findings.title: join() may leave later processes alive when timeout is hit early
_create_process_for_shard is dead code
findings.body: The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase. Restarts are done via `_ensure_processes_alive`, which calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This leftover method just adds noise and may mislead future maintainers into thinking shard-level restart is wired up when it is not.

findings.title: Docstring claims 'one process per shard' but CLI default yields 1 process total
findings.body: The class docstring reads: 'A background multiprocessing manager that polls Redis for new segments to flush and to produce to Kafka. Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' However, the CLI option registered for `process-spans` defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, and the factory forwards that value unchanged. With the production default, self.max_processes == 1, so all assigned shards end up on a single process (process_to_shards_map[0] holds every shard). The docstring is therefore misleading for any deployment that does not explicitly raise `--flusher-processes` to at least len(assigned_shards). Either update the docstring to describe the actual default ('up to N processes; default N=1 means one process handles all shards') or change the CLI default to None so the per-shard behavior is enabled out of the box.

findings.title: CLI help for --flusher-processes contradicts PR goal
findings.body: The new click option is documented as: 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' The PR description says the goal is to 'spawn a process per redis shard'. A reader who wants per-shard processing has no hint from this help text that they must set `--flusher-processes` to a value >= the number of shards; otherwise every shard shares one process. Either rewrite the help to make the relationship to shard count explicit, or change the default so that the stated goal is achieved without operator action.

findings.title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is neutralised by monkeypatch
findings.body: The new line `time.sleep(0.1)` was added with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change', but earlier in the test `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` globally replaces `time.sleep`. The 0.1s sleep is therefore a no-op, and the comment misrepresents what is happening. If the intent was to wait for the threaded flusher to observe the new drift and flush, the sleep needs to be done with a function the monkeypatch doesn't replace (e.g., a busy spin or a different module-level sleep), or the test should `time.sleep` before the monkeypatch and rely on a separate mechanism. As written, the line gives a false sense of safety.

findings.title: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts configuration, not behaviour
findings.body: The new test creates the factory with flusher_processes=2 and 4 partitions, then asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that the total shards across the process_to_shards_map equals 4. It never submits any Kafka message, never advances `current_drift`, never verifies that any of the two flusher threads actually flush a segment, and never asserts how the shards are split between the two processes (e.g., process 0 -> [0,2], process 1 -> [1,3]). It also does not cover the edge cases the new code introduces: flusher_processes=None, flusher_processes=0, flusher_processes >= number of shards, or an explicit per-shard assignment. Without functional coverage the multi-process path could silently regress (e.g., shards never being flushed because the buffer-per-shard mapping is wrong) without any test failing.

findings.title: `if not process:` guard is dead code
findings.body: Inside `_ensure_processes_alive`, the loop has `if not process: continue`, but the dict `self.processes` is only ever assigned via `_create_process_for_shards`, which stores the object returned by `make_process(...)` (either `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` or `threading.Thread`). Both are always truthy after their constructor returns, so the guard is never taken. It can be removed to avoid implying that None/False values may appear here.

findings.title: num_processes=0 with no shards silently disables the flusher
findings.body: `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` evaluates to 0 when the buffer has zero assigned shards. `_create_processes()` then iterates over an empty mapping, so `self.processes`, `self.process_healthy_since`, `self.process_backpressure_since`, `process_restarts`, and `self.buffers` all stay empty. Later in `submit()` the loops over `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` and `self.buffers.values()` are also empty, so no backpressure is ever reported, no `record_stored_segments` metric is emitted, and no process liveness is enforced. If the consumer can ever be constructed with zero partitions (e.g., during a brief rebalance window or misconfiguration), the flusher silently becomes a no-op and segments can pile up in Redis with no operator-visible signal. Adding an explicit guard (e.g., skip creating the SpanFlusher, or raise) would surface this state.
